trust-and-ledgers.q: Which problem does a blockchain solve without a central party?
trust-and-ledgers.e: Without a central ledger keeper, the network must stop a person from spending the same money two times.

trust-and-ledgers.q: When is a normal database the better choice?
o: When many parties do not trust each other
When one trusted party exists and all parties accept it
trust-and-ledgers.e: If a trusted operator already exists, a blockchain adds cost without benefit.

o: Changes to old data are detectable
Data is stored on one server
trust-and-ledgers.e: A change to an old block changes its hash, so all nodes see the break.

trust-and-ledgers.q: A contract receives a wrong delivery date from an outside system. What does the blockchain do?
o: It stores the data; it cannot check if the data is true
trust-and-ledgers.e: Garbage in, garbage out: the chain cannot check real-world truth.

trust-and-ledgers.q: A shared ledger accepts a new entry only if it links to the last one. Complete the pseudo code.
trust-and-ledgers.code:
function append(ledger, entry):
    entry.prev = ____
    entry.hash = hash(entry.prev + entry.data)
    ledger.add(entry)
o: hash of the last entry in the ledger
the name of the person adding it
trust-and-ledgers.e: Each entry stores the hash of the one before it. Changing an old entry changes its hash and breaks every link after it, so tampering becomes visible.

trust-and-ledgers.q: This pseudo code is meant to decide when a blockchain is worth using. One line has the logic reversed. Find it.
code: if only one party writes the data:
use a normal database
if all writers trust one operator:
use a blockchain
if writers do not trust each other and no one should control the record:
consider a blockchain
o: use a normal database (the trusted operator can run it)
trust-and-ledgers.e: If everyone already trusts one operator, that operator can run a database. A blockchain earns its cost only when no single party should control the record.

trust-and-ledgers.q: Put the steps of adding a payment to a shared ledger in order.
steps: Alice signs a payment message with her key
The message is broadcast to the network
Nodes check the signature and the balance
The payment is put into a new block
The block is linked to the previous block by its hash
trust-and-ledgers.e: Sign, broadcast, validate, include in a block, then link the block into the chain.

trust-and-ledgers.q: Complete the double-spend check of a shared ledger.
o: the coin was already spent in an earlier entry
the payment is larger than 1 coin
trust-and-ledgers.e: A coin may be spent only once. All nodes follow one order of entries, so the second payment finds the coin already spent.

trust-and-ledgers.q: Which of the three blockchain tools solves each problem? Complete the line.
trust-and-ledgers.e: Consensus makes all copies of the ledger agree on one order of transactions.

trust-and-ledgers.q: One line in this description of a bank transfer is wrong.
code: the bank can freeze or reverse a payment
the bank checks that the payer has the money
nobody needs to trust the bank
the bank keeps the ledger
o: customers trust the bank to keep the record correctly
trust-and-ledgers.e: A bank is a trusted record keeper. A blockchain replaces that trust with many checking copies.

trust-and-ledgers.q: One line overstates what a blockchain proves in the laptop sale.
code: the ledger proves that the laptop arrived
the payment cannot be quietly changed
the ledger shows that 1 ETH moved from buyer to escrow
anyone can verify the payment later
o: delivery needs an arbiter or an oracle to report it
the ledger proves the laptop's quality
the ledger proves the seller's identity
trust-and-ledgers.e: Outside facts such as delivery are not on chain until someone reports them.

trust-and-ledgers.q: Order how a double spend is stopped on a blockchain.
steps: Alice signs two payments with the same coin
Consensus places one payment first in the agreed order
The second payment finds the coin already spent
trust-and-ledgers.e: One agreed order decides which payment counts.

trust-and-ledgers.q: Order the questions that decide whether a blockchain is worth it.
steps: Do several parties need to write to the record?
Do they want to avoid trusting one of them to keep it?
Must outsiders be able to verify it later?
Only if all answers are yes, consider a blockchain
trust-and-ledgers.e: If one party writes or everyone trusts one operator, a database is better.

hash-functions.q: You hash the same input two times. What is the result?
o: A longer hash the second time

hash-functions.q: You change one character in a document. What happens to its hash?
Which property lets you put the hash of a confidential document on a public chain?
hash-functions.e: Nobody can calculate the document from the hash.

hash-functions.q: Which hash function does Solidity give you as a built-in?
Someone changes data in block 2 of 5. What happens?
o: The hash of block 2 changes and the links of blocks 3–5 break
hash-functions.e: Each block stores the previous block’s hash, so the chain breaks after the change.

hash-functions.q: A notary service proves that a document existed. Complete the line that stores the proof.
hash-functions.e: A hash such as keccak256 gives a fixed-size fingerprint. Anyone can recompute it from the document, but nobody can get the document back from it.

hash-functions.q: This pseudo code checks whether a received file is the original. One line is wrong.
code: expected = stored_hash
actual = hash(received_file)
if actual != expected:
print("File is unchanged")
hash-functions.e: If the hashes differ, the file was changed. Even one changed bit gives a completely different hash (the avalanche effect).

hash-functions.q: Order the steps to prove later that a contract PDF existed today.
steps: Compute the hash of the PDF
Register the hash on chain with a timestamp
Keep the original PDF safely off chain
Compare the new hash with the registered one
hash-functions.e: Only the hash goes on chain. To prove existence later, you hash the same file again and compare.

hash-functions.q: Complete the rule that protects a hash of personal data.
hash-functions.e: Dates of birth have few possible values. A random salt stops attackers from hashing every date and comparing.

hash-functions.q: Complete the line that links a block to the one before it.
hash-functions.e: Each header stores the hash of the previous header, which makes the chain tamper-evident.

hash-functions.q: One property in this list is described wrongly.
code: avalanche: one changed letter changes the whole hash
collision-resistant: similar texts get similar hashes
one-way: you cannot get the input back from the hash
deterministic: same input, same hash
o: collision-resistant: finding two inputs with the same hash is not practical
collision-resistant: every hash is unique by law
hash-functions.e: Similar texts give completely different hashes; that is the avalanche effect. Collision resistance means no two inputs share a hash in practice.

hash-functions.q: One line about Ethereum's hash function is wrong.
code: the output has 256 bits
it is written as 64 hexadecimal characters
Ethereum uses Keccak-256
it is exactly the same as the NIST SHA3-256 standard
o: it differs from SHA3-256 because NIST changed the padding
it is the same as SHA-1
hash-functions.e: Keccak-256 is the original SHA-3 competition winner. The final NIST standard changed the padding, so outputs differ.

hash-functions.q: Order how ETH.BUILD shows that tampering breaks a chain.
steps: Put that hash into block 2 as prev
Block 1's hash changes and block 2's prev no longer matches
hash-functions.e: Changing old data breaks every later link.

hash-functions.q: Order how a court checks a document against a registered hash.
steps: Receive the file from the party
Look up the hash on chain
Read the block timestamp of the registration
Conclude whether this exact file existed at that time
hash-functions.e: The proof needs both the file and the on-chain record.

o: The address that called the function

o: Full control of all keys in the wallet

keys-and-signatures.q: Complete the pseudo code of how a node checks a signed transaction.
o: the account that the message claims to come from
the miner of the last block
keys-and-signatures.e: The signature lets anyone recover the signing address. It must match the account that the transaction claims to come from.

keys-and-signatures.q: These safety rules for a course wallet contain one dangerous line. Find it.
code: write the recovery phrase on paper
type the recovery phrase into a website when asked
use only Sepolia test ETH
create a new wallet only for this course
o: never type or share the recovery phrase anywhere
store the phrase in a screenshot
keys-and-signatures.e: No real wallet, tool or support person needs your recovery phrase. Whoever has it controls the account.

keys-and-signatures.q: Order what happens from creating a key to a payment being accepted.
steps: Derive the public key and the address
Sign a transaction with the private key
A node recovers the address from the signature
The node accepts the transaction because the address matches
keys-and-signatures.e: The private key creates the address and the signatures. Nodes never see the private key; they only check that the signature fits the address.

keys-and-signatures.q: Complete how an Ethereum address is derived.
keys-and-signatures.code:
publicKey = privateKey * G   (elliptic curve)
address   = last 20 bytes of ____
keys-and-signatures.e: The address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the public key.

keys-and-signatures.q: Complete what stops a Sepolia transaction from being replayed on mainnet.
keys-and-signatures.code: signed data includes: to, value, nonce, gas, ____
keys-and-signatures.e: The chain ID is part of the signed data (EIP-155). A Sepolia signature is invalid on mainnet.

keys-and-signatures.q: One line about signatures is wrong.
code: the node recovers an address from the signature
the node needs the private key to check the signature
a changed transaction recovers a different address
the wallet signs with the private key
o: the node needs only the transaction and the signature
the node asks the wallet for the key
the node uses the recovery phrase
keys-and-signatures.e: Verification uses public data only. The private key never leaves the wallet.

keys-and-signatures.q: One step in this wallet backup routine is unsafe.
code: never type the phrase into a website
store the paper somewhere safe and private
write the recovery phrase on paper
take a photo of the phrase as a backup
o: keep a second paper copy in another safe place
upload the photo to the cloud
keys-and-signatures.e: Photos sync to clouds and leak. Whoever sees the phrase controls the wallet.

keys-and-signatures.q: Order how a key pair and an address come to exist.
steps: Multiply it on the elliptic curve to get the public key
Hash the public key with Keccak-256
Take the last 20 bytes as the address
keys-and-signatures.e: Each step is easy forwards and practically impossible backwards.

keys-and-signatures.q: Order what a node checks for an incoming transaction.
steps: Recover the signer's address from the signature
Compare it with the claimed sender
Check that the nonce is the next one
Check that the balance covers value and fee
Accept the transaction into the mempool
keys-and-signatures.e: Signature first, then nonce and balance.

o: The hash of the previous block
consensus.e: The previous hash is the chain link.

consensus.q: Proof of Work is useful because the work is…
o: easy to do and hard to check
hard to do and easy to check
consensus.e: Others can check the result fast without doing the work again.

consensus.e: Slashing gives validators an economic reason to be honest.

consensus.code:
if validator signed two blocks for the same slot:
    ____
o: slash part of the validator's stake
make the validator a proposer next time
consensus.e: Signing two conflicting blocks is an attack. In proof of stake the validator loses part of the stake (slashing).

consensus.q: This summary of proof of work has one wrong line.
code: miners collect transactions into a block
miners search for a nonce so the block hash is below a target
the longest chain with the most work loses
the first valid block is broadcast
o: the chain with the most work wins
the chain with the fewest blocks wins
consensus.e: Nodes follow the chain with the most accumulated work. Rewriting history would need more work than the honest network.

steps: A validator is chosen as proposer for the slot
The proposer builds and broadcasts a block
A committee of validators attests to the block
After enough epochs, the block becomes final
consensus.e: Proposer, block, attestations, then finality after two epochs.

consensus.q: Complete the timing of Ethereum Proof of Stake.
consensus.e: 32 × 12 s = 384 s = 6.4 minutes. Finality takes about two epochs.

consensus.code:
checkpoint is finalised when attestations from ____ of all stake
support it over two epochs
consensus.e: A two-thirds supermajority of stake justifies and then finalises checkpoints.

consensus.q: One line about Proof of Work is wrong.
code: Ethereum still uses Proof of Work for its blocks
miners search for a nonce that gives a small enough hash
nodes follow the chain with the most accumulated work
finding it is expensive, checking it is cheap
o: Ethereum has used Proof of Stake since September 2022
Ethereum uses Proof of Authority on mainnet
consensus.e: The Merge in 2022 switched Ethereum to Proof of Stake.

consensus.q: One line about attacking Proof of Stake is wrong.
code: the protocol detects conflicting votes
the attackers keep their full stake afterwards
the offending validators are slashed
reverting finality needs at least one third of all stake
o: the attackers lose a large part of their stake
the attackers are anonymous and safe
consensus.e: Slashing makes attacks cost the attacker's own capital.

consensus.q: Order the path of a transaction from inclusion to finality.
steps: The transaction is included in a block in slot n
One epoch later the checkpoint is finalised
Exchanges treat the deposit as final
consensus.e: Included after about 12 s, final after about 13 minutes.

consensus.q: Order a Proof of Work block from start to acceptance.
steps: Try nonces until the hash is below the target
Other nodes check the hash and the transactions
consensus.e: Search is costly, verification is quick.

ethereum-evm-gas.e: A contract runs only when an EOA (directly or indirectly) calls it.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: You click a view function in Remix. What happens?
ethereum-evm-gas.e: Reads do not change state, so no transaction is necessary.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: A transaction reverts. What about the gas?
o: You pay for the gas used
ethereum-evm-gas.e: State changes are undone, but the computation already happened.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: How many wei are in 1 ether?
ethereum-evm-gas.e: 1 ether = 10^18 wei. Solidity amounts are in wei.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: Why must contract code be deterministic?
o: All nodes must get the same result
ethereum-evm-gas.e: Every node runs the code; different results would break consensus.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: Complete the formula for the fee of a transaction after EIP-1559.
ethereum-evm-gas.e: Each unit of gas costs the base fee (burned) plus the priority fee (tip to the validator).

ethereum-evm-gas.q: One statement about gas in this list is wrong.
code: unused gas from the gas limit is refunded
a failed transaction costs no gas
writing to storage costs much more gas than reading
a loop over a growing array can run out of gas
o: a failed transaction still pays for the gas it used
a failed transaction is free on mainnet only
ethereum-evm-gas.e: When a transaction reverts, its changes are undone, but the gas used until then is still paid.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: Order how the EVM runs a call to a contract.
steps: The transaction arrives with data for a function
The EVM loads the contract bytecode
It runs the opcodes and charges gas for each
It writes the changed storage if no revert happened
It returns the result and the receipt with logs
ethereum-evm-gas.e: Load code, run with gas metering, commit state only if successful, then produce the receipt.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: Complete the EIP-1559 fee for 50,000 gas.
ethereum-evm-gas.code:
base fee = 8 gwei, priority fee = 1 gwei
fee = 50,000 * ____
ethereum-evm-gas.e: Each gas unit costs base fee plus priority fee: 450,000 gwei = 0.00045 ETH.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: Complete what happens to the base fee.
ethereum-evm-gas.code:
base fee part of the fee -> ____
priority fee part         -> validator
ethereum-evm-gas.e: Since EIP-1559 the base fee is burned.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: One line about account types is wrong.
code: only EOAs can start transactions
EOAs are controlled by private keys
contract accounts hold code and storage
contract accounts can start transactions on their own
o: contracts only act when called by a transaction
ethereum-evm-gas.e: Contracts react; they never start a transaction by themselves.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: One line about the EVM is wrong.
code: the EVM charges gas for each instruction
the EVM can use real random numbers from the node's clock
every node runs the same transactions in the same order
the EVM cannot read the internet
o: the EVM has no access to real randomness or the node's clock
each node uses its own time

ethereum-evm-gas.q: Order the costs of these operations from cheapest to most expensive.
steps: Read a storage slot that was already read in this transaction
Write a new non-zero value to storage
ethereum-evm-gas.e: Arithmetic costs a few gas, storage writes about 20,000, deployment far more.

ethereum-evm-gas.q: Order how a contract call runs.
steps: The wallet signs a call to deposit()
The EVM loads the contract code
The EVM runs the function and charges gas
The new state and the receipt are stored

what-smart-contracts-are.q: A state variable is private. Who can read its value?

what-smart-contracts-are.q: Who used the term “smart contract” first?

what-smart-contracts-are.q: You find a bug in a deployed contract. What can you do?

what-smart-contracts-are.q: Complete the pseudo code of what a smart contract can and cannot decide alone.
o: an oracle or a human arbiter to decide

what-smart-contracts-are.q: One claim about smart contracts is wrong.
code: it runs exactly as written once deployed
a smart contract is a program on a blockchain
it can hold and move tokens by itself
it replaces contract law, so courts are not needed
o: it can be part of a legal contract, but contract law still applies
it is always a legal contract

what-smart-contracts-are.q: Order the life of a smart contract.
steps: Users call its functions with transactions
Its state and events record what happened
what-smart-contracts-are.e: Write, test, deploy, use, and the chain keeps the record.

the money goes to the miner

what-smart-contracts-are.q: One line about smart contracts is wrong.
code: a contract is a program at an address
it can hold and send ETH
it runs exactly as written
it runs on a timer without any transaction
o: nothing runs until someone sends a transaction
it runs every block by itself
it runs when the price changes
